passages.original: De sepulchro quoque sancti Hieronymi simili sollicitudine nobis inquirentibus Arculfus si ait: Sepulchrum sancti Hieronymi, de quo inquiritis, ego conspexi, quod in alia habetur ecclesia, quae extra eandem ciuitatulam in ualle est. fabricata, quae in meridiano latere sita supra memorati dorso monticelli est contermina Bethlemitici.
passages.english: When we likewise asked, with similar care, about the tomb of Saint Jerome, Arculf said: "The tomb of Saint Jerome, about which you are asking, I have seen. It is in another church, which is built outside that same little city in a valley, [and] which lies on the southern side, bordering on the ridge of the above-mentioned little hill of Bethlehem."
passages.notes: The stray "si" after "Arculfus" appears to be a scanning error or misplaced mark (perhaps for "sic") and has been left out. The full stop after "est" before "fabricata" is an evident misplacement and has been ignored. "Bethlemitici" agrees with "monticelli", hence "the little hill of Bethlehem".

passages.original: Idem itaque monticellus Mambre nominatus habet in cacumine campestrem planitiem, ubi ad aquilonalem eiusdem cacuminis partem lapidea magna fundata est ecclesia, in cuius dextrali parte inter duos grandis eiusdem basilicae parietes, mirum dictu, quercus Mambre extat in terra radicata, quae et quercus Abraham dicitur, eo quod sub ea quondam angelos hospitio receperit. Quam sanctus Hieronymus alibi narrat ab exordio mundi usque ad Constantini regis imperium permansisse, et fortassis ideo non dixit penitus defecisse, quia eadem aetate, quamuis non tota illa, sicuti prius fuerat, grandissima quercus monstrabatur, tamen aliqua pars eius permansit in suo stabilita loco.
passages.english: So this same little hill, named Mamre, has on its summit a level plain, where on the northern part of that summit a great church of stone has been built. On its right-hand side, between two great walls of that same basilica, wonderful to say, the oak of Mamre stands rooted in the earth. It is also called the oak of Abraham, because under it he once received angels as guests. Saint Jerome relates elsewhere that it lasted from the beginning of the world up to the reign of the emperor Constantine. Perhaps he did not say that it had perished entirely because, in that same age, although the very great oak was not shown whole as it had been before, still some part of it remained, fixed in its own place.
passages.notes: "regis" (literally "king") is rendered "emperor" because it refers to Constantine.

passages.original: Similiter et ea, quae supra de montis Thabor situ et forma iuxta sancti Arculfi narrationem descripsimus, nullo discrepant modo ab his, quae de situ eiusdem montis et mira rotunditate sanctus Hieronymus narrat. A quo uidelicet Thabor monte usque ad Damascum iter septem dierum Arculfus habuit.
passages.english: Similarly, what we described above about the situation and shape of Mount Tabor, following the account of Saint Arculf, in no way disagrees with what Saint Jerome relates about the situation and wonderful roundness of that same mountain. From this Mount Tabor Arculf had a journey of seven days to Damascus.
